title: Shah: India's Democracy Stands on 76 Years of Unbroken Roots
excerpt: Home Minister credits Constitution, judiciary, and people as the three pillars that have made India's multi-party system a global model.
body:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Sunday declared India's multi-party parliamentary democracy among the most resilient in the world, praising its Constitution and judiciary as indispensable guardians of that stability.

**What Shah Said — and Where:**
Speaking at the launch of Solicitor General Tushar Mehta's two books — 'The Bench, the Bar and the Bizarre' and 'The Lawful and the Awful' — Shah argued that over 76 years, India's democratic roots have only grown deeper. 'Since 1947, changes brought by Parliament and the Assemblies have been accepted without shedding a drop of blood, which shows how deeply rooted democracy is in our country,' he said. Chief Justice Suryakant also attended the event, underlining the rare convergence of the executive and judiciary on one stage.

**Why Institutional Balance Matters:**
Shah framed India's democratic durability around a single idea: institutions designed not for confrontation, but for balance. 'The executive takes decisions, while the judiciary conducts a constitutional review of those decisions,' he explained — a pointed reminder that India's separation of powers functions as a stabiliser, not a battleground. He also stressed that citizens' faith in open courts remains the bedrock of social trust. The Home Minister noted that the three pillars of Constitution, people, and judiciary together ensure that even the weakest voice finds justice.

**What to Watch Next:**
With India navigating a complex geopolitical moment and domestic Bihar elections on the horizon, how the BJP uses this narrative of democratic confidence — especially before state-level votes — will be worth tracking closely.
